question.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+{y}^{′}+\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)y=0.
$$

Suppose ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions and their Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies $W(-1)=6.$ What is $W(2)?$

$W(2)=$ {{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
Abel's identity says that if ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions of

$$
{y}^{″}+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0,
$$

then their Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=-P(x)W(x).
$$

In our equation, the coefficient of ${y}^{′}$ is 

$$
P(x)=1.
$$

Substituting into Abel's identity gives

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=-W(x).
$$

Now, we solve the first-order differential equation for $W:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}^{′} & =-W \\ \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =-\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =\int -\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|W| & =-x+K \\ |W| & ={e}^{K}{e}^{-x} \\ W & =C{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Next, we use the given value $W(-1)=6$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W(-1) & =C{e}^{-(-1)} \\ 6 & =C{e}^{1} \\ C & =6{e}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
W(x)=6{e}^{-1}{e}^{-x}.
$$

Finally, we compute $W(2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}W(2) & =6{e}^{-1}{e}^{-2}=6{e}^{-3}.\end{aligned}
$$
